title: Frontend senior domain rendering strategies
question: Compare client-side rendering, server-side rendering, and static site generation. How would you decide which one, or which mix, fits a given product?
idealAnswer:
Client-side rendering (CSR) ships a mostly empty HTML shell and builds the UI in the browser via JS, it's simplest to build and great for highly interactive apps behind auth, but has a slower time-to-first-content and worse SEO out of the box

Server-side rendering (SSR) generates HTML per-request on the server, giving faster first paint and working SEO, at the cost of server infrastructure, per-request compute cost, and needing hydration on the client to become interactive

Static site generation (SSG) generates HTML at build time, giving the fastest possible delivery (servable from a CDN with no per-request compute) but content can only update on rebuild, making it a poor fit for highly dynamic or personalized data

Incremental static regeneration or similar hybrid approaches try to get static-like performance while allowing content to update without a full rebuild, useful for content that changes but not on every request

The real decision criteria are how dynamic/personalized the content is, how much SEO matters, acceptable infrastructure complexity and cost, and whether different routes in the same app could reasonably use different strategies (many modern frameworks support per-route rendering choice)

Hydration cost itself is a real tax on SSR/SSG apps, the browser must re-execute JS to attach interactivity to already-rendered HTML, this is why partial hydration/islands architectures exist for content-heavy sites
